Plastic Components for Drug Delivery and Combination Devices: What Pharma OEMs Should Evaluate


Pharma OEMs should evaluate drug delivery device components based on function, material requirements, tolerances, manufacturing environment, quality controls, patient interaction, assembly needs and production scale. These factors work together because each component must perform reliably within the complete drug delivery or combination device.


Early evaluation aligns component design and manufacturing with the finished device and production programme. This is especially important in combination product manufacturing and drug delivery injection moulding, where material, process and assembly choices influence performance, manufacturability and scale-up.


### What Should Pharma OEMs Evaluate in Drug Delivery Device Components?


OEMs should assess each factor in the context of the complete device, including the component's function, interfaces and role within the system.


**Evaluation Area** **What OEMs Should Assess** **What to Look for in a Manufacturing Partner**


Component function Role in fit, movement, protection, visibility or device operation. Engineering support that considers component function and device interfaces.


Material requirements Mechanical, chemical, visual, processing and contact needs. Material and processing expertise matched to component function.


Geometry and tolerances Critical dimensions, mating features and tolerance stack-up. FM/DFA, tooling, inspection and repeatable process control.


Cleanliness and manufacturing environment Contamination sensitivity, cleanliness specifications and downstream processing. Controlled or cleanroom production matched to defined cleanliness needs.


Quality system Traceability, inspection, change control, validation and applicable quality expectations. edical-device quality controls supported by relevant certifications and regulatory requirements.


Patient-facing use Handling, tactile characteristics, visibility, robustness and physical interaction. Consistent moulding and assembly for defined patient-facing features.


Assembly and downstream operations Joining, inspection, packaging and other post-moulding steps. Integrated moulding and downstream capabilities where the programme benefits from fewer handoffs.


Production scale Tooling, process development, validation and progression to commercial production. Support that can scale from development through validated production.


Different components will place different weight on these factors. A structural housing, for example, may require different priorities than an autoinjector component involved in movement, fit or dose delivery.


### Start With the Component’s Function and Device Architecture


Before selecting a material or manufacturing process, OEMs should define what the component must accomplish within the device. That role establishes which design and manufacturing characteristics are critical and which allow greater flexibility.


Depending on the device architecture, a moulded component may provide structural support, protect internal features, move or interact with other parts, support visual inspection or form part of the device's external housing. These different roles can create very different manufacturing requirements, even when the components are produced using the same basic process. If the component is patient-facing, identify its role in physical interaction with the device early alongside its mechanical function.


#### Consider Interfaces With Other Components


A component also needs to be evaluated in relation to the parts around it. Features that mate, locate, snap, move or assemble with adjoining components can affect fit and device operation, so those interfaces should be considered early in the design process.


This is particularly important for autoinjector components and other parts that rely on controlled interaction between multiple components. Understanding those relationships helps OEMs identify which dimensions and interfaces are functionally important before making detailed tolerance and tooling decisions.


### How Should Materials Be Selected for Drug Delivery Device Components?


The best material for a drug delivery device component is one that suits its function, manufacturing and assembly needs as well as the conditions it may encounter in service.


OEMs may need to consider factors such as:


- Strength and stiffness
- Dimensional stability
- Chemical compatibility
- Transparency or opacity where required
- Friction and wear
- Mouldability and geometry reproduction
- Assembly method
- Expected environmental exposure
- Applicable patient-, drug- or fluid-contact requirements


The material best for one component may not suit another. For example, a resin selected for a transparent inspection feature may need different properties from one used for a mechanically loaded internal component.


Make material decisions with the manufacturing process in mind. A polymer may meet the component's functional requirements but still create challenges around mouldability, dimensional consistency or assembly. Evaluating material and process requirements together can help identify those trade-offs earlier.


[Sustainability](https://www.sonoco.com/sustainability) goals may also inform material and manufacturing decisions when they align with the component's functional, quality and regulatory requirements. Considerations may include material use, manufacturing waste and appropriate end-of-life pathways.


### Precision Moulding, Tooling and Tolerances Must Work as One System


The most important manufacturing tolerances are those tied to critical dimensions and interfaces that affect fit, movement, assembly or device operation. Appropriate tolerance levels depend on the part's geometry, material, adjoining components and finished-device requirements. Tighter tolerances are not automatically better. They should be applied when necessary to support reliable performance.


For autoinjector components and other precision parts, variation across multiple components can affect how the device functions as a system. Focusing control on critical features avoids applying unnecessarily restrictive tolerances across every dimension.


Reliable drug delivery injection moulding also depends on more than the moulding process itself. Tool design, material behaviour, inspection methods and process controls all influence whether the required dimensions can be reproduced consistently at production scale.


#### Evaluate Tooling and DFM Before Commercial Production


Early design for manufacture and assembly (DFM/DFA) review can identify issues with geometry, mouldability, tolerance, assembly and production scale before tooling is finalised. This allows engineering teams an opportunity to address manufacturing risks earlier, when design changes are generally easier to make.


### Quality Systems and Manufacturing Environment Should Match the Application


A drug delivery injection moulding supplier should have a medical-device quality management system appropriate to the programme, with controls for traceability, inspection, change control, validation and consistent production. The manufacturing environment should also match the component’s intended use, contamination risk and downstream processing.


Relevant certifications, cleanroom classifications, regulatory compliance and facility registrations should be considered individually because each describes a different aspect of the manufacturing and quality environment.


[Cleanroom or controlled-environment manufacturing](https://www.sonoco.com/insights/cleanroom-plastic-components-meeting-medical-grade-manufacturing-standards) is most appropriate when contamination sensitivity, cleanliness specifications, downstream assembly or packaging, or device-specific requirements call for that level of control. ### Patient-Facing Components Add Usability and Assembly Considerations


When designing patient-facing delivery components, OEMs should consider handling, grip, tactile characteristics, visibility, surface quality, robustness and consistent fit within the finished device. Repeatable assembly and manufacturing processes are also important for maintaining these characteristics at production scale.


### From Development Through Assembly and Validated Production


A plastics manufacturer can support a drug delivery device by providing continuity from[early product development and engineering](https://www.sonoco.com/insights/how-sonoco-accelerates-plastic-product-development) through tooling, process development, validation and scale-up.


The value comes from connecting those stages rather than treating them as separate handoffs. Early input can identify manufacturability or assembly risks, while later validation establishes the controls needed for commercial production.


For OEMs, this kind of continuity can be especially valuable in combination-device programmes, where component design, moulding, assembly and downstream operations must remain aligned as the programme moves toward commercial production.

### Frequently Asked Questions About Drug Delivery Device Components


#### Do All Drug Delivery Device Components Need to Be Manufactured in a Cleanroom?


No. Cleanroom manufacturing is appropriate when the component’s contamination-control or cleanliness requirements call for it. Other components may be suitable for standard or differently controlled production environments.


#### What Is the Difference Between a Drug Delivery Device and a Combination Product?


A drug delivery device is designed to administer a drug or other therapeutic product. A combination product brings together two or more regulated product types, such as a drug and a device, within a single product or treatment system. Exact classification depends on the applicable regulatory framework.


#### Can a Plastics Manufacturer Support Both Moulded Components and Device Assembly?


Yes. A plastics manufacturer with the appropriate capabilities and quality controls can support both moulded-component production and downstream device assembly, reducing the need to transfer components between multiple suppliers.


#### When Should a Pharma OEM Involve an Injection Moulding Partner in a New Device Programme?


Early involvement can be beneficial, particularly before material, geometry, tolerance and tooling decisions are finalised. Manufacturing input during development can help identify mouldability, assembly and scale-up considerations before production tooling is committed.
